challenges.title: Academic integrity and unreliable detection
challenges.claim: Generative AI has made academic dishonesty easier, and detection cannot reliably catch it.
challenges.summary: Using AI for assessed work is now near universal among UK undergraduates (94% in HEPI 2026), while admitting to pasting AI text directly is a rising minority (3% in 2024, 8% in 2025, 12% in 2026) and US students name grade pressure (37%) rather than unclear rules (6%) as the main reason peers breach AI rules. Vendor detector output (Turnitin) flags about 11% of 200 million papers as at least 20% AI-written, but detectors are unreliable: Liang et al. found a 61% average false-positive rate on non-native English essays, and students report anxiety about false accusation. Students themselves reject policing (only 21% back AI-detection software) and want education and clearer rules, while 60% worry classmates gain unfair advantage (DEC 2026). Faculty workload is where integrity bites: 71% of instructors with increased workload cite time monitoring for cheating (Tyton).
challenges.severity: Large but poorly measured: prevalence rests on self-report and vendor counts; the best-documented harm is to innocent non-native writers and to instructor workload, and the grade-inflation evidence (see assessment) suggests substitution is real at scale.
challenges.means: Do not lean on detection. The tutor gives hints and never full solutions to graded work, and its logs show the learning process, which matters more than policing the final text; nothing in it penalises non-native writers.

challenges.title: Assessment redesign and grade-signal erosion
challenges.claim: AI erodes what grades and take-home assessment tell us about learning.
challenges.summary: Student perception of change is high and rising (HEPI: 65% in 2026) but only 20% of provosts describe their institution's approach as primarily generative (rethinking what is assessed), 13% as adapting and 8% as defensive. The strongest new causal-style evidence is Chirikov (Berkeley, 2026): at one Texas research university the share of A grades rose 13 percentage points (about 30%) in AI-exposed courses after ChatGPT, more where homework carried more weight, consistent with substitution rather than learning gains. Students themselves see misalignment: only 28% say most assessments reflect AI-enabled workplace needs and 57% report inadequate AI guidance in assessments (DEC 2026). HEPI notes COVID-era take-home formats are a confound for the AI effect.
challenges.severity: Substantial and now quantified for grades at one institution; generalisation is unknown and institutional redesign lags student perception.
challenges.means: Grades are a contaminated signal, so learning is measured on an AI-free post-test (H4), and the tutor withholds answers to graded tasks.

challenges.title: Learning quality, cognitive offloading and skill atrophy
challenges.claim: Using AI can replace the effort that produces learning, so students perform better with it and learn less.
challenges.summary: Controlled evidence splits by tool design: unguarded GPT-4 raised practice scores but cut later unassisted exam scores by 17% (Bastani et al.), while purpose-built tutors raised learning (Kestin et al., Harvard physics; Nigeria RCT +0.3 SD). The OECD 2026 Outlook concludes general-purpose tools improve task performance without necessarily improving learning. Observational and small-n work (Gerlich, n=666 correlational; Kosmyna et al., n=54 EEG preprint) links heavy use to weaker critical thinking or recall but cannot show causation. Students report it too: 19% say they retain less because they rely on AI and 66% worry learning becomes too shallow (DEC 2026), and about 40% of US students are explicitly worried about dependence (IHE 2026).
challenges.severity: Contested and design-dependent: harm appears when AI substitutes for effort, gain when it scaffolds; no long-run evidence in higher education yet.
challenges.means: This is the thesis's core bet: the harm appears when AI substitutes for effort, and the gain when it scaffolds. The guardrails (hints, prerequisite-aware scaffolding from the graph) are the experimental variable, and retention is tested without AI.

challenges.title: Faculty readiness and the student-staff gap
challenges.claim: Staff are not ready to guide students' AI use, and the gap with students is wide.
challenges.summary: Students use AI more than staff can support: only 29% of students say instructors are well equipped (DEC 2026; 17% in US/Canada) even though 64% of faculty report AI-literacy training, and 65% of US higher-ed students say they know more about AI than many instructors (Cengage, vendor). HEPI shows the UK gap narrowing (staff seen as well-equipped 18% to 42% in a year) but only 48% say staff help build career-relevant AI skills in 2026. Leaders cite skills and staff capacity (51% of provosts) and faculty resistance (50%); instructor workload rose for 38% and fell for 11% (Tyton), and faculty intent to use AI in the US and Canada fell from 76% to 67%.
challenges.severity: Persistent and measured by several independent surveys; direction of travel is improving in the UK and worsening in US/Canada faculty sentiment.
challenges.means: Keep the instructor's role small and bounded: reviewing the course graph (RQ1). The graph makes the tutor's knowledge inspectable by staff with little AI training.

challenges.title: Policy and governance lag
challenges.claim: Institutional strategy and policy lag far behind actual use.
challenges.summary: Strategy lags usage: 11% of CTOs report a comprehensive AI strategy, about 1 in 10 provosts a centralized one, 19% of UNESCO-network respondents a formal policy (42% drafting), and only 31% of faculty feel meaningfully involved in AI policy (DEC 2026). Students report mixed clarity: 80% of UK students said policy was clear (HEPI 2025) yet 86% of DEC 2024 respondents were not fully aware of their university's guidelines, and just 10% of US students say their institution handles AI very well (IHE 2026). At school level the pattern is the same: 19% of US K-12 teachers report a school AI policy, and schools with one see a 26% larger time dividend (Gallup).
challenges.severity: Governance is clearly behind adoption in leader self-reports; measures of 'clarity' depend on who is asked and how.
challenges.means: A course-scoped tutor that cites its source for every answer is easier to bring under an institutional policy than an open chatbot; its data use is documented up front.

UNESCO's 2025 survey of UNESCO Chairs reports one in four had already encountered AI ethical issues including authorship disputes and bias in research. challenges.means: The thesis discloses its own AI use (as Iranian ministry rules require), and every graph triple keeps its provenance.

challenges.title: Productivity and tutoring gains
challenges.claim: Well-designed AI tutoring produces real learning gains.
challenges.summary: RCT-grade evidence shows gains from structured AI tutoring: Kestin et al. (Harvard physics, median learning gains over double those of active learning, 0.73-1.3 SD), Nigeria RCT (+0.31 SD, +0.21 SD on end-of-year exam), . Students report better understanding (HEPI 49% better experience; Chegg 50%), but vendors fund much of the survey evidence. Effects come from single courses and short pilots and are likely upper bounds.
challenges.severity: Strong where the tool is pedagogically designed; weak for open chatbots.
challenges.means: The gains come from tutors built on pedagogy (Kestin, Nigeria); H4 tests whether graph retrieval adds to that. Effects of 0.3 to 1 SD from single courses are treated as upper bounds.

challenges.title: Personalisation
challenges.summary: Students are lukewarm on AI-built courses (18% say they are more valuable than traditional ones, DEC 2024) and only 15% say AI is integrated into many of their courses (DEC 2026). Provosts rank personalised learning among the least common institutional AI uses (8%). OECD notes purpose-built, teacher-designed tutors show most promise.
challenges.severity: Promise largely unrealised at scale in leader and student data.
challenges.means: Prerequisite edges allow concept-level personalisation, but evidence of value at scale is thin, so the thesis claims answer quality and learning gain, not personalisation.

challenges.title: Administrative efficiency
challenges.claim: AI saves staff time and makes institutions more efficient.
challenges.summary: The clearest institutional payoff is individual productivity and administration: 55% of CTOs and 39% of provosts name it, and US K-12 teachers using AI weekly estimate 5.9 hours saved per week (Gallup). Institution-wide transformation is rare (8% of provosts), and for higher-ed instructors net workload rose for 38% and fell for 11% (Tyton) because monitoring and redesign cost time.
challenges.severity: Real at individual level; rarely institution-wide.
challenges.means: Secondary for the thesis: instructor time saved on answering questions can be logged, but the primary outcome is student learning per hour of study.
